title: Draw a right-angled triangle on an Etch A Sketch, turning both knobs together for the slanted side
instruction: Draw a right-angled triangle on the Etch A Sketch, starting at the dot near the lower left of the screen: a line 80 mm to the right, then 60 mm straight up, then a straight slanted line back down to the dot, turning both knobs at the same time for the slanted line. Do not lift, tilt or shake the toy. Then let go of both knobs and move both arms away.
context: An Etch A Sketch draws continuously as its two knobs move a stylus. Drawing a straight diagonal requires coordinating both knobs, including regrips and direction changes.
setup: Units mm. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. Two YAM arms with parallel grippers (pads 94 apart when open), bases at (0, +305) and (0, -305), ready pose, grippers open; one overhead camera and one camera on each wrist (320 x 176). Wooden table top, nothing else on it. 1) Etch A Sketch, the full-size classic (Spin Master; any full-size red-framed one with a 155 x 108 drawing area will do): red plastic frame 227 x 186 x 23.7 (26.6 at the raised lip round the screen), corners rounded 7.8, about 454 g, lying flat on the table screen up with its centre at (380, 0), its long sides along y and its knobs on the side nearest the robot, so that a player sitting at the robot would see it the right way up. Screen 161 x 115, silver-grey; the stylus can reach 155 x 108 of it. Two white ribbed knobs, 28.2 across and 12.3 tall, tops 40.4 above the table, centres at (305, +95) (left knob, moves the line left and right) and (305, -95) (right knob, moves it up and down). Turning the left knob clockwise, seen from above, moves the line to the right; turning the right knob clockwise moves it up (away from the robot). One knob turn moves the line 35.5. After a knob changes direction it turns about 20 degrees before the line moves (the slack of the toy's strings). The knobs have no stops and stay where they are left. 2) The start dot: a single dot already drawn on the screen 30 from its left edge and 20 from its bottom (robot-side) edge, at (346, +51), with the stylus on it. The triangle to draw has its corners at the dot, 80 to the right of it (346, -29) and 60 above that (406, -29). 3) Tape marks on the table at the toy's four corners. The start layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged on the toy's screen after the trial with a ruler and a close-up photo (a loupe or a phone's macro photo shows the real line, about 0.5 mm wide), and from the trial video for the toy and the grippers. Coordinates in mm from the start dot, X to the right, Y up the screen; the ideal triangle is A (0, 0), B (80, 0), C (80, 60). A side is covered over a 1 mm piece of its length when some of the drawn line within 2 mm of the side lies over that piece. 0.25: the bottom side AB covered over at least 70 of its 80 mm. 0.5: in addition the upright side BC covered over at least 50 of its 60 mm. 1.0: in addition the slanted side CA covered over all of its 100 mm (so the line comes back to within about 3 mm of the dot), with no step in it: more than 5 mm from its two ends, no straight piece of the line longer than 1 mm runs within 10 degrees of horizontal or vertical (the slanted side itself runs at 37 degrees to the horizontal; a 1 mm piece is two widths of the real line, plain under a loupe or in a macro photo with a protractor overlay). Turning one knob and then the other leaves such steps at every change; turning both together leaves none. A stray line (any drawn point more than 2 mm from every side of the triangle) caps the score at 0.25. The sides may be drawn in any order and either direction. The score is 0 if the toy is lifted, tilted or shaken (any bottom corner 2 mm or more off the table), pushed so that its centre is 10 mm or more from its marks, or turned 5 degrees or more, or if any part of the robot touches the toy (knobs included) during the last second of the trial. In simulation the same rules are applied to the logged stylus path. The trial ends at the run limit, or 1 s after full score is reached with both grippers off the toy. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: First turn the knobs until the stylus is at the start point, 30 mm from the screen's left edge and 20 mm from its bottom edge (check with a ruler where the line ends). Then erase the picture by turning the toy screen down and shaking it; the stylus is held by its strings and stays where it is. Lay the toy back on its tape marks screen up, draw the dot with a tiny back-and-forth of one knob and check its place with the ruler again (redo if it is more than 1 mm off), and turn each knob back by about 10 degrees, half its slack, which does not move the stylus. Return both arms to ready with grippers open. In simulation: seed 0, no jitter; the toy is put back on its marks, both knobs at zero with their slack centred, the line cleared to the start dot, and the scorer's memory starts fresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Lab-Arena (PhysX, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control) at the toy's measured size. The toy is one free articulation: the frame (a box collider with four lip colliders round the screen, on the table by friction) and two knobs on revolute joints about the vertical with no stops. Each knob is a plain cylinder 28.2 across and 12.3 tall that the grippers hold by real finger contact; nothing attaches a gripper to a knob, and the knobs turn only when the fingers turn them. A knob resists turning with a drag capped at 0.03 N m (an estimate: no figure is published). Inside the real toy each knob winds strings that pull the stylus along two rails; here that drive is a kinematic rule: each knob angle passes through a 20 degree dead band (the string slack) and moves the stylus 35.5 mm per turn, and at the ends of its travel the stylus stops while the knob keeps turning, as on the real toy. The drawn line is a stated rule standing in for the aluminium powder being scraped off the glass (a material response): every stylus position is drawn on the screen as a dark line 3 mm wide, wider than the real line (under 1 mm), so that it shows in the 320 x 176 overhead view; the scorer uses the stylus path, not the drawn width. Erasing by shaking is not modelled (lifting or tilting the toy scores 0). What the cameras see are display meshes with no collision: the red frame with rounded corners and its lip, the silver-grey screen and ribbed white knobs with a small mark on top; the maker's printed name is left off. Measured figures: frame and knob sizes, knob positions, screen borders, stylus travel and 35.5 mm per turn; the 20 degree slack is from two published knob-driving projects; the 454 g is from retail listings; the turning drag, the split of the mass, friction values and the knob turning directions are estimates (see README).
